newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel says Clinton right to stand up to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Havel says Clinton right to stand up to Russia.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton was right not to give in to Russian demands on the expansion of NATO, and enlargement will go ahead, no matter how much Moscow tries to stop it, Czech President Vaclav Havel said on Sunday.

"NATO's enlargement will continue, following its own logic and reasons. It is not aimed at Russia. Russia can dislike it as much as it wants, but it is unable to prevent it from happening," Havel said in his regular weekly address.

Enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) was the key topic at the Helsinki summit on Friday. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are widely tipped to be invited to join after the Madrid summit in July.
At the Helsinki summit, Clinton and his Russian counterpart Boris Yeltsin "agreed to disagree" on expanding NATO, though Clinton said expansion would go ahead on schedule at the Madrid summit.

Russia bitterly opposes the expansion of the former Soviet Union's old Cold War foe to territory once under the sway of the Moscow-dominated Warsaw Pact. At the summit, Yeltsin reiterated Russia's view that expansion was a mistake.

Analysts say Moscow is trying to gain as many concessions as possible from the United States in the process of NATO expansion, and perhaps to forestall a further widening of the alliance, especially to former Soviet Republics.
But Havel said that while Russian concerns should not stop the process, the security alliance should build a true partnership with Russia and work on peaceful cooperation.

"However, at the same time this does not mean that one should accommodate or go along with any quirk and geopolitical wish of Russia brought about by its specific traditions," the playwright-turned-President said.
He said Russia had "never been totally sure where its territory starts or ends" and was inclined, even if unintentionally, to create buffer zones around itself.
"It seems that Russia has traditionally distrusted Western structures and suspected them of being aimed against Russia," he said.

"It is important not to succumb to this way of seeing things, not to allow it to be imposed on us, not to come up with compromises, but to stand one's ground firmly and explain why NATO wants to enlarge itself. It is necessary to be firm in this. I think that this is exactly what happened in Helsinki."
